frus-1861-d2:
Secretary of State Jeremiah Black sent a general letter to all United States ministers abroad on 28 February 1861. It is document 2 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861, the papers laid before Congress with the President's annual message.

Black served the last weeks of President Buchanan's term, as states left the Union one by one. A circular to every minister at once set one line for all posts to follow. It shows Washington speaking to the whole world in a single voice at the edge of civil war. Black left office within days, which makes this circular a last act of the old cabinet.
frus-1862-d2:
In a report dated 22 November 1861, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 2 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The letter comes from the autumn of the war's first year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1863p1-d2:
On 30 November 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The letter is document 2 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. Seward's letters gave Adams his orders for the hardest brief in the service.

Washington's aim in London was plain: keep Britain from backing the South or letting warships slip out of its yards. Seward wrote to a man he trusted, in terms that mixed firm claims with care not to push Britain too far. This early letter in the volume shows the tone of that talk, set by the secretary himself at the start of a long winter.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d2: President Roosevelt wrote to Marshal Stalin on May 5, 1943, in a letter preserved as Document 2 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The two leaders had never met, and their exchanges that spring worked toward a first face-to-face summit. The record gives sender, date, and place in the volume, but no subject line, so the letter's business must be read from its text. It opens the long paper road to Tehran.
frus-1944-quebec-d2:
President Roosevelt answered Prime Minister Churchill on March 20, 1944, two days after the message that opens the Quebec volume. The State Department printed the reply in the Foreign Relations volume for the 1944 Quebec Conference.

Prompt answers were the rhythm of the Roosevelt-Churchill partnership: a question from London, a decision or a counter-proposal from Washington, often within days. Spring 1944 pressed both men with the invasion of France and the politics of liberated Europe. For readers, this early exchange shows the correspondence warming up for the decisions that the September conference would have to settle in person.
frus-1945-50-intel-d2:
E. R. Baker of the Bureau of the Budget staff wrote to Martin, the bureau's assistant director for estimates, on 24 August 1945. The Budget Bureau spoke for the president on money and on the shape of agencies. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Budget papers matter in fights over new agencies, since the bureau could starve or feed a plan before Congress ever saw it. Baker's memorandum shows the money men entering the intelligence debate at its very start. Readers tracing how the postwar spy system was built should watch the Budget Bureau's thread. Its quiet memos often decided which grand designs survived contact with cost and law.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d2: Ambassador Averell Harriman reported to President Roosevelt from Moscow on 18 July 1944. His message stands as document 2 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences, issued by the Department of State. Harriman was Washington's main eyes inside the Soviet capital, and reports like this one shaped what the president knew before the Big Three met again.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d2:
Truman answered Churchill on May 9, 1945, agreeing that a meeting of the three heads of government was desirable. Questions on which no decision or common understanding had been reached needed action. But he set one condition of style: he much preferred that the request for a tripartite meeting come from Stalin, not from either of them.

Perhaps, he suggested, Churchill had means to induce Stalin to propose or request such a meeting. Meanwhile, Truman intended to hold to the American reading of the Yalta agreements. He would stand firmly on the announced attitude toward all questions at issue. The new President's first Potsdam move was patience, publicly armed.
frus-1951-54IranEd2:
A second edition of the Iran volume for 1951–1954 stands as its own record in the series. Its arc matches the first: efforts to understand Mosadeq from February 1951, then the July 1952 crisis and its aftermath. The same four blocks structure the book.

Planning and execution of Operation TPAJAX fill the third block, from March to August 1953. The aftermath runs to December 1954. Readers can set the two editions side by side to see the record as reissued. The subject, the overthrow of a government with American help, keeps both in demand. The edition's added papers deepen the coup record with names once held back.
frus-1969-76ve15p2Ed2:
This second, revised edition of Part 2 of Volume E-15 covers Western Europe from 1973 to 1976 in the 1969-1976 series. It keeps the first edition's shape: a long regional section, then country sections. Canada, Portugal, the Nordic countries, Spain, the United Kingdom, West Germany, and France all return. The revision adds a section on Italy, with documents 344 through 382. A Scowcroft memo of April 26, 1976, on food aid sits in the regional run.

Portugal's revolution and Spain's change of regime anchor the country papers. The Italy section adds the Communist vote's rise and U.S. concern over it. The edition supersedes the first for this part.
frus-1977-80v09Ed2:
This second, revised edition of Volume IX, in the 1977-1980 series, covers the Arab-Israeli dispute from August 1978 to December 1980. The first chapter covers the Camp David summit of August and September 1978. Two chapters then follow the talks on the Egyptian-Israeli peace treaty, to March 1979. A fourth covers the search for a broader peace in 1979. The last is titled Stalemate, and runs to January 1981.

Talk records show Sadat and Carter trading warm words even in hard sessions. The papers trace the treaty text clause by clause. Autonomy talks for the West Bank and Gaza fill the later chapters. The volume ends with those talks stalled.
tob-0038-d2:
Book II of the Church Committee's 1976 final report turns from foreign spying to intelligence work aimed at Americans. The Senate committee, led by Frank Church, spent over a year digging into agency files. What it found at home shocked the country.

The book documents FBI domestic surveillance, the COINTELPRO campaigns against civil rights and antiwar groups, and the opening of mail and tapping of dissenters. It argues that secret agencies, left unchecked, had broken laws and trampled rights. Its call for charters and standing oversight helped set the rules that still govern domestic intelligence work.
tob-0039-d2:
The third microfilm roll of the Doctors' Trial transcript continues the Nuremberg case of 1946 to 1947. Twenty-three physicians and administrators stood charged with war crimes and crimes against humanity. Their alleged acts were medical experiments performed on camp prisoners without consent.

On this roll, testimony and exhibits build the prosecution's account session by session. Nothing is summarized; the record keeps questions, answers, and rulings as spoken. Trials of this size live or die on paper, and the rolls keep that paper whole. The case ended with death sentences for some defendants and a code of ethics for research on human beings.
